briefs.hpv:
Adolescent Vaccines

the 11 to 12 year platform, human papillomavirus (HPV) series rules, meningococcal boosters and influenza seasonIs the age gate open, is the series already complete, and is it the season?

Platform and gatesHPV series rulesPractice
Bottom line

When every option is a real vaccine, decide by eligibility. There are only three gates: age platform, series already complete, and season; check them in that order. A date buried in line one of the stem is data.

  • Adolescent platform: at 11 to 12 years, Tdap (tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid and acellular pertussis), HPV vaccine and MenACWY (meningococcal conjugate vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y) come due together.
  • Catch-up principle: every encounter is a vaccination opportunity, including a sports physical.
  • Series complete: a child up to date at 9 has finished every infant and early-childhood series: hepatitis B, MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) and pneumococcal conjugate.
  • Season: influenza vaccine is due every year; it is gated by timing, not eligibility (below).
  • HPV dose count: age at the first dose sets the series. A first dose at 9 to 14 years: 2 doses, at 0 and 6 to 12 months. At 15 or older: 3 doses, at 0, 1 to 2 and 6 months. Immunocompromising conditions, including HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection: 3 doses regardless of age.
  • Never restart: a vaccine series is not restarted, regardless of the time between doses; a delayed dose is simply given late, resuming where you left off. Minimum intervals matter; there is no maximum interval.
  • Meningococcal: MenACWY booster at 16, when the risk period begins; MenB (serogroup B meningococcal vaccine) is separate: shared decision-making at 16 to 23 when not at increased risk.
Platform and gates
Each option and the gate it fails: June, age 11, up to date at 9
VaccineWhen it is givenWhy not at this visit
TdapSingle dose at 11 to 12 yearsIt is the answer
InfluenzaEvery year; September and October are generally good timesIt is June: not the season
MMR12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 yearsSeries complete before age 9
Pneumococcal conjugateInfant series at 2, 4, 6 and 12 to 15 monthsComplete; no routine dose in a healthy 11-year-old
Hepatitis BBirth, 1 to 2 months, 6 to 18 monthsSeries complete in infancy
High-risk meningococcal schedule Asplenia – anatomic or functional, including sickle cell disease: MenACWY becomes a 2-dose primary series (first dose at 2 years or older), at least 8 weeks apart · HIV infection, persistent complement deficiency or a complement inhibitor such as eculizumab – the same 2-dose MenACWY primary series · MenACWY boosters – at age 7 or older, a booster every 5 years while the risk remains · MenB – added from age 10 for asplenia, persistent complement deficiency or a complement inhibitor (not for HIV infection)
Influenza timing Influenza most commonly peaks from December through February. September and October are generally good times, ideally by the end of October. July and August can be considered for a child who needs only one dose; most adults, especially those 65 years and older, and pregnant women in the first or second trimester should generally not be vaccinated that early (in July or August), because protection may decrease over time. A child 6 months to 8 years old with fewer than 2 doses (at least 4 weeks apart) before July 1 of the current season, or an unknown history, needs 2 doses separated by at least 4 weeks, the first as soon as vaccine is available.
HPV series rules
Series mechanics Two independent rules – the age at the first dose sets the series length; a delay never restarts the series · Too-early dose – a dose given 5 or more days before the minimum interval does not count and is repeated; for the 2-dose series the minimum interval is 5 months · Catch-up – recommended through age 26, with shared decision-making at 27 to 45 · Lifestyle details – sexual activity, prior HPV exposure and abnormal Pap results do not change the recommendation; vaccinate anyway, since the vaccine still protects against strains not yet acquired
Schedule status, October 2026 A January 2026 CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) revision recommended a single HPV dose. A federal court stayed that revision in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts keeps the 2-dose series when started at 9 to 14, and the AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) also recommends two doses, starting at 9 to 12; check the CDC site for the current schedule. On retired exam items, the classic keyed answer remains two doses if started before 15 and three if at 15 or older or immunocompromised: the posted schedule and the exam answer currently agree.
Practice
  1. 11-year-old girl is seen in June for a pre-participation sports evaluation Her vaccines were up to date at age 9; she has had none since and is healthy, with no travel planned Afebrile · BP 106/66 mm Hg → Tdap → age 11 opens the adolescent platform, and Tdap is the one offered vaccine whose scheduled slot is now. Influenza vaccine is excluded by timing, not eligibility: she is due for it every year, just not in June. Measles-mumps-rubella was finished at 4 to 6 years
  2. 12-year-old girl is seen for a well visit and receives her first dose of HPV vaccine today She is healthy, takes no medications and has no chronic illness Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → Two doses → the age at the first dose sets the series: a first dose at 9 to 14 years means 2 doses, at 0 and 6 to 12 months. Three doses are for a first dose at 15 or older or an immunocompromising condition. The single dose is the January 2026 revision, which a court has stayed; the posted schedule keeps 2 doses
  3. 11-year-old girl is seen for a well visit and receives Tdap today She completed all childhood vaccine series on schedule and is healthy, with no medications Afebrile · HR 82/min · BP 104/64 mm Hg → HPV and MenACWY → the 11 to 12 platform is three vaccines: Tdap, HPV vaccine and MenACWY. The pneumococcal conjugate and hepatitis B series finish in infancy, with no routine dose in a healthy 11-year-old, and the MMR and varicella series both end at 4 to 6 years
  4. 17-year-old boy is seen for a sports physical and receives his first dose of HPV vaccine He is healthy, with no chronic illness and no medications Afebrile · HR 64/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg → Three doses → a first dose at 15 or older means 3 doses, at 0, 1 to 2 and 6 months; the 2-dose series is only for a first dose at 9 to 14 years
  5. 16-year-old boy is seen for a sports physical before his junior year He received MenACWY at age 11 and has had no meningococcal vaccine since He is healthy Afebrile · BP 118/70 mm Hg → MenACWY booster dose → MenACWY is given at 11 to 12 with a booster at 16, when the risk period begins; a healthy adolescent does not repeat the primary series. MenB is separate: 16 to 23 by shared decision-making, preferably at 16 to 18
  6. 15-year-old girl is seen for a sports physical She received one dose of HPV vaccine 14 months ago and has had no doses since Healthy; no medications Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg → Give the second dose today → a series is never restarted, regardless of the time since the last dose: a delayed dose is simply given late, and there is no maximum interval. Her first dose came before 15, so the second dose completes a 2-dose series; one dose alone is complete only under the stayed January 2026 revision
  7. 11-year-old girl is seen in early October for a pre-participation sports evaluation Her vaccines were up to date at age 9; she has had none since and is healthy Afebrile · BP 102/66 mm Hg → Give Tdap and influenza vaccine at this visit → both are due now: age 11 opens the Tdap slot, and September and October are generally good times for influenza vaccine, ideally by the end of October. Influenza most commonly peaks from December through February, so waiting until December gives up protection. Every encounter, including a sports physical, is a vaccination opportunity, and the rest of the 11 to 12 platform, HPV vaccine and MenACWY, is due at this visit too
  8. 13-year-old boy with HIV infection, taking antiretroviral therapy, is seen for a routine visit He receives his first dose of HPV vaccine today and is otherwise well Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg → Three doses regardless of age → immunocompromising conditions, including HIV infection, need 3 doses even when the series starts at 9 through 14 years. No additional dose is recommended once a series is complete, so there is no booster at 18
  9. 11-year-old boy with sickle cell disease and functional asplenia is seen for a well visit His vaccines are otherwise up to date; he has had no meningococcal vaccine Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL → MenACWY as a two-dose primary series, plus MenB → asplenia changes the schedule: anatomic or functional asplenia, including sickle cell disease, makes MenACWY a 2-dose primary series at least 8 weeks apart, with a MenACWY booster every 5 years from age 7 while the risk remains, and adds MenB from age 10. HIV infection, persistent complement deficiency and complement inhibitors such as eculizumab bring the same 2-dose MenACWY primary series
  10. 12-year-old girl is seen for a well visit and review of her vaccine record Her first HPV vaccine dose was at age 11; the second was given 4 months later She is healthy; no medications Afebrile · BP 100/62 mm Hg → Repeat the second dose → for a series begun at 9 to 14 years the minimum interval is 5 months, and a dose given too soon is repeated: a dose given 5 or more days before the minimum interval does not count. Repeating one dose is not restarting the series, and two doses are needed: a single dose is complete only under the stayed January 2026 revision
  11. 11-year-old girl is seen for her adolescent vaccines with 2 days of rhinorrhea She is eating and playing normally; no ear pain or cough T 37.8 °C · HR 92/min · lungs clear → Vaccinate today → mild illness is not a contraindication: mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotics and breastfeeding are not reasons to delay these vaccines, so Tdap, HPV vaccine and MenACWY are all given today, and none waits for her to be afebrile. A moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is the precaution
  12. 28-year-old woman asks whether she should still receive HPV vaccine She never received any dose as a teenager Her cervical cytology last year was normal Afebrile · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Shared decision-making through age 45 → routine catch-up runs through age 26; at 27 to 45 years the decision is shared, completing 2 doses if started at 9 to 14 or 3 if started at 15 or older. Sexual activity, prior HPV exposure and abnormal Pap results do not change the recommendation
  13. 11-year-old girl who arrived from abroad last month is seen for a school-entry visit Her parents report she had all childhood vaccines; no written records are available Afebrile · BP 100/64 mm Hg → Vaccinate as though unimmunized → only written records count as evidence of vaccination (self-report is accepted only for influenza vaccine): undocumented means unvaccinated, and a verbal report does not count. Every encounter is a vaccination opportunity, so she starts today rather than waiting for records
  14. 15-year-old girl is seen for a well visit and has never received HPV vaccine She is not sexually active; her parent asks whether it is too late Afebrile · BP 108/70 mm Hg → Begin the HPV series today → catch-up HPV vaccination is recommended through age 26, and a start at 15 means 3 doses, at 0, 1 to 2 and 6 months. Sexual activity, prior HPV exposure and abnormal Pap results do not change the recommendation; the vaccine still protects against strains not yet acquired
  15. 8-year-old boy is seen in mid-August for a pre-participation sports evaluation He has never received influenza vaccine; this season's vaccine arrived last week He is healthy Afebrile · BP 100/62 mm Hg → Give the first of two doses today → a child 6 months to 8 years old with fewer than 2 doses (at least 4 weeks apart) before July 1 of the current season, or an unknown history, needs 2 doses separated by at least 4 weeks, so the first is given as soon as vaccine is available. At 9 or older one dose is enough, and July and August can be considered for a child who needs only one dose; September and October are generally good times, ideally by the end of October
Not a reason to wait Mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotics and breastfeeding are not contraindications; a moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is a precaution. Undocumented means unvaccinated: only written records count, and verbal report does not.
Common wrong answers An interval calculation: two years since the last visit baits one for a series with no remaining doses. Pneumococcal or hepatitis B: the recommendations feel unsettled enough that something seems owed, but both series finished in infancy. Restarting a delayed series.
Pairs with Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications covers the infant schedule, the rotavirus age limits and pertussis contraindication versus precaution. Ask: is this an age-platform question or a series-mechanics question?
Transferable rule

When every option is a real vaccine, decide by eligibility: age platform, series already complete, then season. When lifestyle details appear alongside a guideline, check whether they actually change the algorithm; usually they do not.
